newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt marks first year, but tough times ahead. [CORRECTED 21:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Italy govt marks first year, but tough times ahead. [CORRECTED 21:30 GMT]

text.p: Italy's first centre-left government for half a century celebrated a year in power on Sunday but its achievements have been overshadowed by constant political battles and the certainty that more turbulence lies ahead.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi, whose government is the 55th since World War Two, reeled off a list of successes at a weekend gathering of his centre-left Olive Tree coalition.

Inflation is down to its lowest level for 28 years, interest rates have fallen by more than three points, Italy's deficit to Gross Domestic Product ratio has narrowed sharply and Prodi said conditions were ripe for "upturn and development".
In the past, Prodi has trumpeted such achievements as proof that a year of the bitter budgetary medicine he has prescribed to try to tame Italy's unruly state finances is working.
But with more unpopular taxes on the horizon in the 1998 budget, details of which were leaked in the press, and the road to European monetary union still rocky, Prodi opted for modesty.
"The fruits are not miraculous or extraordinary but more that this, in a year, couldn't have been done," he said.
Despite progress on economic reform, European Union finance ministers last week appoved a sharply-worded Commission report blasting Italy for unsustainable budgetary measures.
Elsewhere, a political battle is brewing on welfare reform and the government is under fire from the judiciary.
A recent stunt by armed separatists in Venice has increased the pressure for federal reform and Italy faces diplomatic headaches over a security force it is leading in Albania.

Prodi, a mild-mannered former economics professor with little past political experience, has had a sharp learning curve since his alliance of former Christian Democrats, ex-communists and Greens Party members won last April's general election.
The government was sworn in on May 18, 1996.

One of Prodi's biggest lessons has been how to deal with Communist Refoundation, the hard-left party whose support he needs for a parliamentary majority but whose ideology has repeatedly put it on collision course with the government.
Despite calling 22 do-or-die confidence votes, Prodi has only been in real danger once -- when Refoundation dramatically broke ranks over an Italian-led security force in Albania in April.
Prodi eventually survived thanks to support from the opposition centre-right, but the mission's future is now unclear because of a mounting crisis over planned Albanian elections.
Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti has promised a fight to the death if necessary on what he calls "the mother of all issues" -- reform of Italy's welfare state.

Refoundation opposes any cuts in social spending and Bertinotti insists compromises must be found. Economists say reform of the unwieldy system is vital for Italy's chances of founder membership of economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
Prodi has made entry into economic and monetary union his chief goal and has said he will resign if his strenuous efforts to clean up Italy's finances do not succeed.

He has introduced close to 100 trillion lire ($60 billion) in cost-cutting measures in his year in office , including unpopular taxes to hammer the deficit-GDP ratio towards the three percent required for EMU entry.
High taxes were one of the main grievances raised at a recent anti-government rally in Milan organised by centre-right at which Prodi was styled as Dracula, sucking Italy's blood.
His government has also come under attack over planned legal reforms from prosecutors in Milan, where vast corruption scandals that felled the old ruling class blew up in 1992.

They said the government was trying something that not (corrects by inserting dropped word 'not') even disgraced former prime minister Bettino Craxi, one of the most reviled figures in the whole corruption scandals, had attempted.
Prodi's promises of a clean, new Italy included reform of the constitution to give more stable government and federalism.

The Venice protest, in which a small armed band seized the belltower until police ended the siege peacefully, has spurred the special parliamentary commission examining constitutional reforms, which must complete its work by the end of June. ($1=1,668 lire)
